justification: Forming a fresh judgement first: this is a strong, original article that clearly outperforms the current top results for 'code coverage explained'. Microsoft Learn's own coverage tutorial is mostly project-scaffolding instructions with one screenshot and no dark mode; Fowler's TestCoverage bliki is prose-only with no runnable demonstration. This article instead builds one running example (Temperature -> Freezing -> HeatAdvisory) that walks a reader from a 100%-covered-but-wrong assertion, through branch coverage, through a boundary bug two full-branch-coverage tests still miss, into mutation testing applied by hand once Stryker.NET is honestly shown (via a real executed failing run, not an assertion) not to work against this pillar's file-based programs. I re-derived every branch/method coverage number by hand against the shown ternary structure and they are all correct (e.g. the two-comparison 'severe' rewrite genuinely has 4 branches, not 3, and the article correctly explains why). I ran `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/testing/code-coverage.md` myself seven times in a row (isolated, no other process touching this worktree): all seven passed (`blocks=36 executed=18`), which is strong evidence round 1's flaky `id=killed` block is genuinely fixed -- it has been split into two separate single-`[Fact]` programs (`killed-below`, `killed-above`), removing the shared-class ordering race entirely, with prose that now explicitly explains why. I independently re-fetched every primary source this article quotes (Microsoft Learn's coverage and mutation-testing pages, both Fowler bliki posts, Stryker.NET's intro, Coverlet's README) and checked each quotation and attribution against the live page text myself: the round-1 fabricated quotation ('extensive JUnit test coverage') is gone, replaced with verbatim fragments of Fowler's actual sentence; the round-1 misattributed Marick quote ('If a part of your test suite is weak...') is now correctly credited to Brian Marick, and I confirmed on the raw page that this is in fact the second and last Marick quotation on the page, immediately before the 'Further Reading' section, so 'quotes Marick a second time on the way out' is accurate; the dotnet-coverage 'such as console or Blazor' quote now matches the live page exactly, character for character. Those were the two blockers and the major that capped round 1, and all three are cleanly resolved, not papered over. However, forming my own judgement surfaced a new factual error round 1 did not catch, and it caps this round the same way: the exercise 'Predict which mutant survives' claims both of its listed mutations against the three-test, `<=`-fixed version of `Freezing.Classify` are killed. I ran the first one myself -- changing the threshold literal from `32` to `33`, i.e. `fahrenheit <= 33 ? "Freezing" : "Not freezing"`, against the article's own three tests (20, 32, 50) -- and all three tests pass (Total: 3, Failed: 0). The mutant survives: none of the three fixed test values fall in the (32, 33] gap the mutation opens, so `Classify(32)` still returns "Freezing" exactly as it did before the mutation, contradicting the article's own worked answer that 'a 33 threshold would make 32°F fall on the "Not freezing" side.' That claim is simply false, and it is false about the article's own central subject: a subtle, off-by-one boundary mutation slipping past a full-branch-coverage suite is exactly the failure mode this page spends 700 lines teaching readers to hunt for, and here its own answer key gets that hunt wrong. Per the binding rubric a factual error caps the technical score at 7 regardless of the article's real strengths elsewhere, so despite everything above being fixed cleanly, round 2 cannot score higher than 7.0.

issues.location: lines 791-799, the `::::exercise[Predict which mutant survives]` block and its `:::solution`, mutation 1 ("Change the threshold literal from `32` to `33`.")
issues.problem: The solution states 'Both are killed' and explains mutation 1 by claiming 'a 33 threshold would make 32°F fall on the "Not freezing" side, so that test fails.' This is factually wrong and I verified it by actually running the mutated program: with `fahrenheit <= 33 ? "Freezing" : "Not freezing"`, `Classify(32)` still evaluates `32 <= 33` as true and returns `"Freezing"` -- unchanged from the original -- so `AtThreshold_IsFreezing` (which asserts `Classify(32) == "Freezing"`) still passes, and so do the other two tests at 20 and 50, since neither of them lies in the (32, 33] range this mutation actually affects. Running all three tests against this mutant gives `Total: 3, Failed: 0` -- the mutant survives, it is not killed. The article's own thesis is that a suite can look complete (full branch coverage, even a boundary test at 32) and still miss a one-off boundary shift; this exercise's answer key asserts the opposite of what actually happens for exactly that kind of shift, in the one place a reader is asked to reason it out for themselves.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either correct the stated outcome for mutation 1 to 'survives' and explain why (none of 20/32/50 lands in the gap a 32->33 shift opens; only a test at 33 itself, or between 32 and 33, would catch it) -- which would make the exercise a stronger, more on-theme demonstration of the article's own point -- or replace mutation 1 with one that is actually killed by the three tests as written (e.g. changing the threshold to `31`, since `Classify(32)` with `fahrenheit <= 31` flips to `"Not freezing"` and the `AtThreshold_IsFreezing` assertion then fails). Whichever fix is chosen, re-run the mutated program against the three tests by hand (or restate it as a `run` block) before handing off again, the same way the rest of the article verifies every other coverage and mutation claim.

issues.location: lines 83 and 136, Coverlet is introduced first ("Coverlet ... describes itself as providing 'line, branch and method coverage'") but every actual measurement on the page uses `dotnet-coverage` instead
issues.problem: The article names Coverlet in its very first solution block to establish the line/branch/method vocabulary, then silently switches to `dotnet-coverage` for every real measurement without ever saying why Coverlet itself isn't the tool used. A reader who knows Coverlet is the more commonly-documented option (it's what Microsoft's own coverage tutorial builds around) is left to infer, rather than being told, that Coverlet's collection paths (coverlet.collector via `dotnet test`, or coverlet.msbuild) assume a project file the same way Stryker.NET later is shown to, which is presumably the actual reason a file-based program needs `dotnet-coverage` instead.
issues.fixLooksLike: Add one sentence near line 136, where `dotnet-coverage` is first introduced as 'the coverage tool this whole page uses', noting that Coverlet's own collection paths (`dotnet test --collect` or the MSBuild package) likewise assume a `.csproj`, which is why a file-based program needs `dotnet-coverage`'s process-level attach instead -- the same honest-limitation treatment the article already gives Stryker.NET.
